cat.etymology: From Old Northern French cat (variant of Old French chat) from Late Latin cattus.

livre.etymology: From Old French livre, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin liber, librum.

pie.etymology: From Old French pie, from Latin pica, feminine of picus (“woodpecker”).

nu.etymology: From Old French nu, from Latin nūdus.

absent.etymology: From Old French ausent, relatinized on the model of its ancestor, Latin absēns (“absent, missing”), present active participle of absum, abesse (“be away, be absent”).

absolution.etymology: From Old French absolution, from Latin absolūtiō, absolūtiōnem (“acquittal”), from absolvō, absolvere (“absolve, acquit”), from ab (“from, away from”) + solvō, solvere (“release, loosen, dissolve, take apart”).

libre.etymology: From Old French, borrowed from Latin līber (“free”).

jeudi.etymology: From Old French jeudi, jusdi, from Latin Jovis diēs or Iovis diēs, a variant of diēs Iovis (“day of Jupiter”).

Inherited from Old French noit, from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.

four.etymology: From Old French forn, from Latin furnus.

point.etymology: From Old French point, from Latin punctum.

man.etymology: From Old French main, mein, man, from Latin manus (“hand”).

port.etymology: From Old French port, borrowed from Latin portus (“port, harbour”).

jour.etymology: From Old French jor, from Late Latin diurnum.

langue.etymology: From Old French langue, from Latin lingua.

glosses_en: France (a country located primarily in Western Europe)
France.etymology: From Old French France, from Late Latin Francia.

digital.etymology: Borrowed from Latin digitālis, from digitus (“finger, toe”) + -ālis (“-al”).

glosses_en: Afghanistan (a landlocked country between Central Asia and South Asia)

gas.etymology: From Old French gars, nominative singular form of garçon.

accent.etymology: From Old French acent, from Latin accentus, from ad + cantus (“song”).

glosses_en: USSR (initialism of Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, official name of Soviet Union: a former transcontinental country in Europe and Asia (1922–1991), now split into Russia and 14 other countries; in full, Unnion d'Républyiques Socialistes Soviétiques)
Anguilla (an archipelago and overseas territory of the United Kingdom in the Caribbean Sea)
Aruba (an island, dependent territory, and constituent country of the Netherlands, in the Caribbean Sea)

ache.etymology: From Old French ache, from Latin apium (“parsley, celery”).

glosses_en: to look at oneself in the mirror
mither.etymology: From Old French mirer (“to look at; to watch”), from Latin mīror, mīrārī (“be amazed at”).

donner.etymology: From Old French doner, from Latin dōnō, dōnāre (“give a present; bestow, grant”), from dōnum (“gift, present”).

glosses_en: tree mallow (Malva arborea, syn. Lavatera arborea)
mauve.etymology: From Old French mave (“mew”), from Old English mǣw (“mew, seagull”) or Old Norse már, mávar (compare Icelandic mávur), from Proto-Germanic *maihwaz, *maiwaz (“seagull”).

pi.etymology: From Old French pié, from Latin pēs, pedis, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds.

an.etymology: From Old French an, from Latin annus.

picture.etymology: From Old French picture, borrowed from Latin pictūra (“the art of painting, a painting”) (compare the inherited Old French form peinture), from pingō, pingere (“paint; decorate, embellish”), from Proto-Indo-European *peyḱ- (“spot, color”).

glosses_en: air (mixture of gases that make up the earth's atmosphere)
second-person singular present indicative of aver

parent.etymology: From Old French parent, from Latin parēns, parentem, from pariō, parere (“bring forth, give birth to, produce”).

cousin.etymology: From Old French cosin, from Latin cōnsobrīnus.

expression.etymology: Borrowed from Latin expressiō, expressiōnem (“a pressing out”).

rue.etymology: From Old French rue, developed figuratively from Latin ruga (“wrinkle”).

martyr.etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυρ (mártur), later form of μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).

taupe.etymology: From Old French taupe, from Latin talpa.

civil.etymology: Borrowed from Latin cīvīlis, from cīvis (“citizen”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey- (“to lie down, settle; home, family; love; beloved”).

glosses_en: first-person singular present indicative of aver

us.etymology: From Old French uis, from Latin ostium.

boulevard.etymology: From Old French bollevart (“promenade, avenue, rampart”), from German Bollwerk or Middle Dutch.

sale.etymology: From Old French sale (“dull, dirty”), from a Germanic source, from Proto-Germanic *salwaz (“dusky, dark, muddy”), from Proto-Indo-European *salw-, *sal- (“dirt, dirty”).

bouton.etymology: From Old French boton, from Late Latin *bottōnem, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *bautō (“that which pushes up, bump, knob”).

ail.etymology: From Old French, from Latin allium.

train.etymology: From Old French train (“a delay, a drawing out”), from trainer (“to pull out, to draw”), from Vulgar Latin *tragināre, from *tragere, from Latin trahō, trahere (“pull, draw”, verb).

borne.etymology: From Late Latin bodina, butina, from Transalpine Gaulish.

have.etymology: Borrowed from Old Norse háfr (“net”), from Proto-Germanic *hēb-, *hēf-, an ablaut form of *hafjaną (“to have; take; catch”). Related to English dialectal haaf (“a pock-net”).

pigeon.etymology: Inherited from Old French pyjon, from Late Latin pīpiōnem (“chirping bird”), from Latin pīpiāre (“to chirp”).

laid.etymology: From Old French laid, leid (“unpleasant, horrible, odious”).

lent.etymology: From Old French, from Latin lentus (“slow, sluggish”).

mal.etymology: From Old French mal, from Latin male.

canal.etymology: From Old French canal, from Latin canālis (“channel; canal”).

bra.etymology: From Old French bras, from Vulgar Latin *bracium, from Classical Latin bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn).

tout.etymology: From Old French tot, from Latin tōtus.

sang.etymology: From Old French sanc, from Vulgar Latin sanguem, alteration of Latin sanguinem, accusative of sanguis.

cause.etymology: From Old French cause, borrowed from Latin causa.

change.etymology: Borrowed from French change and English change.

vif.etymology: From Old French vif, from Latin vīvus (“alive, living”).

piano.etymology: Borrowed from English piano and French piano.

et.etymology: From Old French et, from Latin et.

if.etymology: From Old French if, from either Frankish *īw (from Proto-Germanic *īhwaz) or Gaulish *iwos (“yew, yew tree”) (from Proto-Celtic *iwos, compare Breton ivin, Old Irish eó, Welsh ywen); in either case from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyHw-. See yew

long.etymology: From Old French long, a back-formation from longe, longue, the feminine form of Early Old French lonc, from Latin longus.

vote.etymology: Borrowed from English vote, from Latin vōtum, from voveō, vovēre (“vow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wegʷʰ-.

glosses_en: his, her, its (used to qualify masculine nouns)
san.etymology: From Vulgar Latin sum, from Classical Latin suum.

u.etymology: From Old French ueil, from Vulgar Latin oclus, from Latin oculus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”).

femme.etymology: From Old French fame, feme, fenme, femme, from Latin femina; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-éh₂ (“(the one) nursing, breastfeeding”), derivation of the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, suckle”).

pour.etymology: Inherited from Old French por, from Late Latin pōr, from Latin prō.

content.etymology: From Old French, borrowed from Latin contentus (“having been held together, contained”), from contineō, continēre (“hold or keep together, surround, contain”).

franc.etymology: From Old French franc (“free, genuine, sincere”), from Late Latin Franc (“a Frank”), of Frankish origin.

acater.etymology: From Old Northern French acater, from Vulgar Latin *accaptāre (“accept, purchase”). Compare French acheter.

liège.etymology: From Old French, from Vulgar Latin *levius, from Latin levis (“light (in weight)”).

pomme.etymology: From Old French pome, pume, from Latin pomme, from Latin pōma, plural of pōmum (“fruit”), from Proto-Italic *poomos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂po-h₁ém-os (“taken off”).

rein.etymology: From Old French rein, reins, from Latin rēn, rēnes.

cœur.etymology: From Old French cuer, from Vulgar Latin *corem m, from Latin cor n.

un.etymology: Inherited from Old French uns, from Latin ūnus (“one”).

deux.etymology: From Old French deus, from Latin duōs, masculine accusative of duo.

quatre.etymology: From Old French quatre, from Latin quattuor, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.

huit.etymology: From Old French uit, from Latin octō, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw.

neuf.etymology: Inherited from Old French nuef, from Latin novem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥.

dix.etymology: From Old French dis, from Latin decem, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥.

onze.etymology: Inherited from Old French onze, from Latin ūndecim.

douze.etymology: From Old French doze, from Latin duodecim.

treize.etymology: From Old French treize, treze, from Latin trēdecim.

quatorze.etymology: From Old French quatorze, from Latin quattuordecim.

seize.etymology: Inherited from Old French seize, from Latin sēdecim.

quarante.etymology: From Old French quarante, from Late Latin quarranta, from Latin quadrāgintā.

musique.etymology: From Old French musique, from Latin musica, from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “art of the Muses”), derived from Μοῦσα (Moûsa, “Muse”).

couleur.etymology: From Old French color, from Latin color, colōrem.

glosses_en: ring which is used to fix an animal

li.etymology: From Old French li, from Vulgar Latin *illui, a Vulgar Latin dative of Classical Latin ille.

abbé.etymology: From Old French abé, borrowed from Latin abbās, abbātis (“abbot”).

si.etymology: From Old French si, from Latin si (“if”).

co.etymology: From Old French colp, coup, from Vulgar Latin *colpus, from Classical Latin colaphus (“blow with the fist; cuff”), from Ancient Greek κόλαφος (kólaphos, “blow, slap”).

pot.etymology: From Old French pot (“pot”), from Vulgar Latin pottum, pottus (“pot, jar”), from Frankish *pott, from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot, jar, tub”), from Proto-Indo-European *budn- (“a kind of vessel”).

la.etymology: From Old French la, from Latin illa(m).

sole.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sola, from Latin solea.

démocratie.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French democratie, from Medieval Latin dēmocratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (dēmokrătĭ́ā).

maire.etymology: From Old French maire, from Latin maior (“elder”).

profit.etymology: From Old French profit, from Latin profectus (“advance, progress, growth, increase, profit”).

restaurant.etymology: Either inherited from Old French or borrowed from French.

gras.etymology: From Old French gras, from Late Latin crassus.

mission.etymology: From Old French mission, borrowed from Latin missiō, missiōnem.

communion.etymology: From Old French comunion, borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin communio, communionem, from Latin communis.

Christ.etymology: Borrowed from Latin Christus, from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós), proper noun use of χριστός (khristós, “the anointed one”).

vodka.etymology: From English vodka, from Russian во́дка (vódka), diminutive of вода́ (vodá, “water”).

net.etymology: From Old French net, from Vulgar Latin *nittus, from Latin nitidus (“shiny”).

à.etymology:

Proto-Italic *ad

From Latin ad.

vent.etymology: From Old French vent, from Latin ventus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

glosses_en: the tailboard finial on a Jersey horse van

trente.etymology: From Old French trente, from Latin trīgintā.

glosses_en: a male given name from Latin [in turn from Ancient Greek], equivalent to English Nicholas

virgule.etymology: Borrowed from Latin virgula, diminutive of virga (“rod, branch”).

scorpion.etymology: From Old French scorpion, from Latin scorpiō, scorpiōnem, from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos).

crocodile.etymology: Inherited from Old French cocodril, from Medieval Latin cocodrillus, from Classical Latin crocodilus, from Ancient Greek κροκόδειλος (krokódeilos).

sort.etymology: From Old French sort, from Latin sors, sortem.

front.etymology: From Old French front, from Latin frōns, frontem.

fo.etymology: From Old French fol, from Latin follis.

pale.etymology: From Old French pale, from Latin pallidus (“pale, pallid”).

course.etymology: From Old French cours, from Latin cursus (“course of a race”), from currō (“run”).

main.etymology: From Old French main, mein, man, from Latin manus (“hand”).

service.etymology: From Old French servise, (compare French service), borrowed from Latin servitium, from servus.

glosses_en: Malta (an archipelago and country in Southern Europe, in the Mediterranean Sea)
Malta (the largest island in the Maltese Archipelago)

dans.etymology: From Vulgar Latin dē intus (“from inside, from within”). Cognate with French dans.

seine.etymology: From Latin sagēna, from Ancient Greek σαγήνη (sagḗnē, “dragnet”).

est.etymology: From Old French, from Old English ēast.

sans.etymology: From Old French sans, senz, sens, from Latin sine conflated with absentia in the sense "without".

pirate.etymology: From Old French pirate, from Latin pīrāta, from Ancient Greek πειρατής (peiratḗs), from πεῖρα (peîra, “trial, attempt, plot”).

harpe.etymology: From Old French harpe, from Late Latin harpa, from Proto-Germanic *harpǭ.

yi.etymology: From older *ye, from Old French ueil, from Vulgar Latin oclus, from Latin oculus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”).

neu.etymology: From a variant of Old French nuef, from Latin novus.

nord.etymology: From Old French norht, north, nort (“north”), from Old English norþ (“north”).

direct.etymology: Borrowed from Latin dīrēctus, perfect passive participle of dīrigō, dīrigere (“straighten, direct”). Compare the inherited drait, drouait.

vain.etymology: From Old French vain, from Latin vānus (“empty”).

arme.etymology: From Old French arme, from Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms”).

dragon.etymology: From Old French dragon, from Latin dracō, dracōnem, from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn).

beet.etymology: From Old French beste, from Latin bēstia.

trio.etymology: Borrowed from English trio, French trio.

latte.etymology: From Old French latte, late, from a Germanic source, probably Frankish *latta.

hus.etymology: Possibly a Germanic borrowing, as no obvious cognates exist in Romance (the expected inheritance would be Old French porte, such as Jersey dialect porte). Compare Old Norse hús (“house”).

glosses_en: Mongolia (a Mongolian-speaking geographic region in East Asia, including the country of Mongolia (Outer Mongolia), the autonomous region of Inner Mongolia in China, and sometimes also Buryatia, Tuva and the Altai Republic in Russia)

barbe.etymology: From Old French barbe, from Latin barba, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂.

gris.etymology: Derived from Old French or Old Occitan, in either case from Proto-Germanic *grēwaz (“grey”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰregʰwos (“grey”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to glow, shine”).

né.etymology: From Old French noi and its variants, from Latin nix, nivem.

ambulance.etymology: Borrowed from English ambulance and French ambulance.

hangar.etymology: Borrowed from French hangar, from Frankish *haimgard.

fils.etymology: From Old French fils, fil, from Latin fīlius.

pays.etymology: From Old French païs, from Late Latin pāgēnsis (“inhabitant of a district”), derived from Latin pāgus (“countryside; district”).

carte.etymology: From Latin charta (probably borrowed), from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “papyrus, paper”).

muscle.etymology: Borrowed from Latin mūsculus (“a muscle”, literally “little mouse”), from Ancient Greek μῦς (mûs, “mouse, muscle, mussel”).

niche.etymology: From Old French niche, from nichier (“make a nest”), from Latin nīdus (“nest”).

large.etymology: From Old French large, from Latin largus (“abundant, plentiful, copious, large, much”).

catamaran.etymology: Borrowed from English catamaran, from Tamil.

futur.etymology: From Latin futūrus, future active participle of sum, esse.

crucifix.etymology: From Old French crocefis, crucefix, borrowed from Latin crucifixus.

crotchet.etymology: From Old French crochet (“small hook”), from croc (with diminutive suffix -et), from Old Norse krókr (“hook”).

dos.etymology: From Old French dos, from Vulgar Latin dossum, from Latin dorsum.

nor.etymology: From Old French norht, north, nort (“north”), from Old English norþ (“north”), from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą (“north”), from Proto-Indo-European *ner- (“lower, bottom; to sink, shrivel”).

re-.etymology: From Old French re-, from Latin re-.

extra-.etymology: Borrowed from Latin extra (“outside, except, beyond”, adverb and preposition), from exter (“being on the outside”).

quart.etymology: From Old French quart, from Latin quartus.

crêpe.etymology: Substantivisation of Old French crespe, from Latin crispus.

whisky.etymology: From English whisky, ultimately from Old Irish uisce.

programme.etymology: From Late Latin programma (“a proclamation, edict”), from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma, “a written public notice, an edict”).

en-.etymology: From Old French en-, from Latin in-, prefixation of Latin in (“in, into”); see en.

fin.etymology: From Old French fin, from Latin finis.

soprano.etymology: Borrowed from English soprano, from Italian soprano, from Vulgar Latin *superānus, from Latin super.

sobre.etymology: From Old French sobre, borrowed from Latin sōbrius.

saint.etymology: From Old French saint, from Latin sanctus (“holy”).

glosses_en: Alps (a mountain range in Western Europe)

courge.etymology: From Old French cohourge, ultimately from Latin cucurbita, perhaps via Vulgar Latin *cucurbica.

chambre.etymology: Borrowed from French chambre, from Old French chambre, from Latin camera.

prêt.etymology: From Late Latin praestus, from the adverb praesto.

vivre.etymology: From Old French vivre, from Latin vīvō, vīvere, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti (“to live, be alive”).

monstre.etymology: From Old French monstre, borrowed from Latin mōnstrum.

dent.etymology: From Old French dent, from Latin dēns, dentem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts.

por.etymology: From Old French porc, from Latin porcus, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”).

motion.etymology: Inherited from Old French motion, mocion, borrowed from Latin mōtiō (“movement, motion”).

faux.etymology: From Old French faulz, the plural of fault, ultimately from Latin falsus.

coupe.etymology: From Late Latin cuppa, from Latin cūpa.

ko.etymology: From Old French col, from Latin collum (“neck”).

noeud.etymology: From Old French neu, from Latin nōdus.

faire.etymology: From Old French faire, from Latin facere.

fer.etymology: From Old French fer, from Latin ferrum.

frère.etymology: From Old French frere, from older fredre, fradre, from Latin frāter, frātrem, from Proto-Italic *frātēr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.

soeur.etymology: From Old French suer, from Latin soror, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.

traire.etymology: From Old French traire, from Early Medieval Latin tragō Latin trahō (“to pull”).

lettre.etymology: From Old French letre, from Latin littera.

mettre.etymology: From Old French metre, from Latin mittō, mittere.

naître.etymology: Inherited from Old French naistre, from Latin nascere.

dû.etymology: From Latin dūrus, from Proto-Indo-European *deru-, *drew-. Compare French dur.

su.etymology: From Old French sud, su (“south”), from Old English sūþ, from Proto-Germanic *sunþrą.

doux.etymology: From Old French dous, from Latin dulcem, accusative of dulcis (“sweet”).

fou.etymology: Inherited from Old French forn, from Latin furnus.

folle.etymology: Old French fole, feminine of fol (“mad”) from Latin follis.

goût.etymology: From Old French goust, from Latin gustus.

ou.etymology: From Old French ou, from Latin aut.

small-spotted catshark, lesser spotted dogfish (Scyliorhinus canicula)

tuer.etymology: From Old French tuer, from Latin tūtāri (“avert, ward off”).

duvet.etymology: From Old French duvet (“down, the feathers of young birds”), alteration of dumet, dumect, from Old French dum, dun (“down, feathers”), from Old Norse dúnn (“down, down feather”).

vite.etymology: From Old French viste, of disputed origin; see vite.

haut.etymology: From Old French hault, haut, halt (“high, tall, elevated”), a conflation of Frankish *hauh, *hōh (“high, tall, elevated”) and Latin altus (“high, raised, profound”).

page.etymology: From Old French page, from Latin pāgina (“page, strip of papyrus fastened to others”).

litter.etymology: From Old French liter, luitier, from Latin luctārī. Compare French lutter.

avant.etymology: From Old French avant, from Late Latin ab ante (“before, in front of”), from Latin ab (“from”) + ante (“before”).

aver.etymology: From Old French aveir, archaic form of avoir, from Latin habēre (“have, hold, possess”).

ciel.etymology: From Old French ciel, from Latin caelum.

feu.etymology: From Old French feu, from Latin focus (“hearth”).

palais.etymology: From Old French, from Vulgar Latin *palātium, an alteration of Classical Latin palātum (“palate”) with influence from palātium (“palace”).

Italie.etymology: From Latin Ītalia (“Italy”), from Ancient Greek Ἰταλία (Italía).

camp.etymology: From Old Northern French camp (compare Old French champ), from Latin campus, from Proto-Indo-European *kamp- (“to bend; crooked”). Compare French champ.

capel.etymology: From Old French capel, from Early Medieval Latin cappellus, diminutive from Late Latin cappa.

d'.etymology: From Old French de, from Latin dē.

triste.etymology: Inherited from Old French triste, borrowed from Latin trīstis.

pais.etymology: From Old French, from Latin pīsum, from Ancient Greek πίσον (píson).

gallon.etymology: From Old Northern French galon, from Late Latin galum, galus (“measure of wine”), from Vulgar Latin *galla (“vessel”), possibly from Gaulish *galla, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“goblet”).

ange.etymology: From Old French angle, ange, angre, from Late Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger”).

glosses_en: Cyprus (an island and country in the Mediterranean Sea, normally considered politically part of Europe but geographically part of West Asia)

yo.etymology: From Old French yaue, ewe, euwe, egua (“water”), from Latin aqua (“water”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water, flowing water”).

glosses_en: A letter used in writing Norman representing /s/.

père.etymology: From Old French pedre, pere, from Latin pater, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.

abat.etymology: From Old French abatre, from Late Latin abbattere, from Latin battere.

glosses_en: more, -er (used to form comparatives of adjectives)
pus.etymology: From Old French plus, from Latin.

glosses_en: -al (of or pertaining to; adjectival suffix appended to various words, often nouns, to make an adjective form)

porter.etymology: From Old French porter, from Latin portō, portāre.

prison.etymology: From Old French prison, from Latin prehensiō, prehensiōnem (“seizing, apprehending, arresting, capturing”).

chapelle.etymology: From Old French chapele, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin cappella, diminutive of cappa.

haler.etymology: From Old French haler (“to pull, haul”)

année.etymology: From Old French anee, equivalent to an + -ée; an (“year”) from Latin annus (“year”). Perhaps alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *annāta, from Latin annō, annāre, compare French année, Walloon anêye, Italian annata.

lundi.etymology: From Old French lundi, from Latin *Lūnae diēs, variant of diēs Lūnae (literally “day of the Moon”).

collège.etymology: From Old French college, from Latin collēgium.

fossile.etymology: From Latin fossilis (“something which has been dug up”), from fodio (“to dig up”).

paître.etymology: From Old French paistre (“to graze”), from Latin pāscō, pāscere (“feed, nourish, maintain, support; pasture, drive to pasture, attend; feed, supply, cultivate, let grow; graze, browse”).

touot.etymology: From Old French tot, from Latin totus.

confirmer.etymology: From Latin cōnfirmō, cōnfirmāre (“make firm, establish, strengthen, fortify, mature, confirm”), from con- (“with, together”) + firmō, firmāre (“strengthen, fortify”).

soûler.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *satullāre, diminutive of Latin saturō, saturāre (“fill to repletion, sate, satisfy”).

navet.etymology: From a diminutive of Old French nef (“turnip”), from Latin napus.

mât.etymology: From Old French mast, from Frankish *mast, from Early Medieval Latin mastus, from Proto-Germanic *mastaz.

foudre.etymology: From Old French foudre, from Latin fulgura, nominative plural of fulgur.

tortue.etymology: Cf. French tortue. Probably from Old Occitan tortuga, tartuga, from Late Latin tartarucha, feminine form of tartaruchus, a mythological spirit of Greek origin, from Ancient Greek ταρταροῦχος (tartaroûkhos, “inhabitant of Tartarus”), from Τά

dromadaire.etymology: From Old French dromedaire, from Late Latin dromedārius (“kind of camel”), from Classical Latin dromas, from Ancient Greek δρομὰς κάμηλος (dromàs kámēlos, “running camel”), from δρόμος (drómos, “race course”).

propagande.etymology: From New Latin propāganda, short for Congregātiō dē Propagandā Fide, "congregation for propagating the faith".

sauveur.etymology: Borrowed from French sauveur, from Late Latin salvātor.

pétale.etymology: From Ancient Greek πέταλον (pétalon), from πέταλος (pétalos, “broad, flat”).

glosses_en: Used to form agent nouns from verbs.

tuyau.etymology: From Old French tuyau, tueil, tudel (“tube, pipe”), from Frankish *thūta (“pipe”), from Proto-Germanic *þeutǭ (“pipe, channel, flow”), from *þeutaną (“to howl, roar, resound”), from Proto-Indo-European *tu-, *tutu- (“bird-cry, shriek”).

doryphore.etymology: Borrowed from French doryphore, from New Latin Doryphora, its former genus.

mêler.etymology: From Old French mesler, from Early Medieval Latin misculāre, derived from Latin miscēre.

tilleul.etymology: From Old French tilluel, from Vulgar Latin *tiliōlus, from Latin tilia. Cf. also Old French til.

généalogie.etymology: From Old French genealogie, from Late Latin genealogia, from Ancient Greek γενεαλογία (genealogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”).

glosses_en: a male given name, equivalent to English Moses

contester.etymology: From Latin contestor, contestārī (“call to witness”).

architecte.etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, “master builder”), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + τέκτων (téktōn, “builder”).

glosses_en: a female given name, equivalent to English Amber

geindre.etymology: From Old French giembre, from Latin gemō, gemere.

corrompre.etymology: From Old French corrompre, borrowed from Latin corrumpō, corrumpere (“pervert, corrupt, deprave, infect; spoil, rot; taint, contaminate; tempt, seduce”).

donzelle.etymology: From Old French damoisele, from Vulgar Latin *domnicella, from Classical Latin domina (“mistress”), from domus (“house”), from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm, from root *dem- (“to build”).

glosses_en: Yugoslavia (a former country in Southeastern Europe in the Balkans, now split into 6 countries: Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, and Slovenia)
Yougoslavie.etymology: Borrowed from French Yougoslavie, from Serbo-Croatian Jugoslavija.

hypothèque.etymology: From Latin hypothēca (“pledge given as surety for a loan”), from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē).

gril.etymology: From Old French greïl, graïl (“gridiron”), from graïlle (“grate, grating”), from Latin crātīcula (“gridiron”), diminutive of crātis (“hurdle, wickerwork”), from Proto-Indo-European *kor(ə)t-, *krāt- (“to weave, twist, wattle; wicker”).

valeu.etymology: From Old French valur, valeur, from Late Latin valor, valorem, from Latin valeō.

garanti.etymology: From Old French guarantie, from the verb guarantir (“to protect, assure, vouch for”), from Vulgar Latin *warantīre, from *warantus, a form of *warīre, from Frankish *warjan.

frit.etymology: From Old French fruit, from Latin fructus.

fache.etymology: From Old French fache, from Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“face, shape”).

épilepsie.etymology: From Old French epilepsie, from Latin epilēpsia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιληψία (epilēpsía).

meule.etymology: From Old French mole, muele, from Latin mola.

mitaine.etymology: From Old French mitaine, possibly from mite (“pet name for a cat”) (see the French entry above).

dictateur.etymology: Borrowed from French dictateur, from Latin dictātor (“a chief magistrate”), from dictō (“dictate, prescribe”), from dīcō (“say, speak”).

glosses_en: a diminutive of the male given name Âbréhan or Âbra-am

symbole.etymology: From Latin symbolus, symbolum (“a sign, mark, token, symbol, in Late Latin also a creed”), from Ancient Greek σύμβολον (súmbolon, “a sign by which one infers something; a mark, token, badge, ticket, tally, check, a signal, watchword, outwar

abondant.etymology: From Old French abondant, from Latin abundāns, present participle of abundō (“abound or overflow in”).

ôter.etymology: From Old French oster, from Latin obstō, obstāre, from ob (“before, in front”) + stō, stāre (“stand”).

panser.etymology: From Old French panser, an alternative form of penser (“to think”).

nouer.etymology: From Old French noer, from Latin nōdāre.

poupe.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *puppa, alteration of Latin puppis, possibly through Ligurian (Genoese) popa, cf. French poupe.

braire.etymology: From Old French braire, from Gaulish.

pélican.etymology: Borrowed from French pélican, from Latin pelecānus, from Ancient Greek πελεκάν (pelekán).

cyprès.etymology: From Latin cupressus, cypressus, cyparissus, from Ancient Greek κυπάρισσος (kupárissos).

peis.etymology: From Old French peis, pois, from Latin pīsum, from Ancient Greek πίσον (píson).

abcès.etymology: From Latin abscessus (“a going away; gathering of humors, abscess”), perfect passive participle of abscēdō, abscēdere (“go away, depart”), from abs (“away from”) + cēdō, cēdere (“go”).

banqueroute.etymology: Borrowed from French banqueroute, from Italian bancarotta.

rithe.etymology: From Old French rire, from Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre.

bâtard.etymology: From Old French bastard (“child of a nobleman by a woman other than his wife”), from Medieval Latin bastardus (“illegitimate child”), from Proto-Germanic *banstuz, *bunstuz (“a bond”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie, bind”).

âpre.etymology: From Old French aspre, from Latin asper, possibly a borrowing.

godet.etymology: From Middle French godet, from Dutch kodde (“piece of cylindrical wood”).

trique.etymology: From an Old Northern French [Term?] derivative of Old French trichier.

rubis.etymology: From Old French rubi, rubin, borrowed from Medieval Latin rubinus, from Latin rubeus (“red, reddish”), from rubeō, rubēre (“be red, ruddy”).

pichet.etymology: From Old French pichier, bichier, from Late Latin pīcārium, bīcārium, itself possibly from bacarium, or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos).

vessie.etymology: From Old French vessie, from Latin vessīca, variant of vēsīca.

veine.etymology: From Old French veine, from Latin vēna.

hanneton.etymology: Borrowed from French hanneton, from Frankish *hano (“rooster”).

réception.etymology: Borrowed from Latin receptiō, receptiōnem (“the act of receiving; reception”), from recipiō (“receive”), from re- (“back”) + capiō (“to hold”).

diacre.etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διάκονος (diákonos, “servant, minister”).

Jerri.etymology: From Old Norse, compound of Geirs (“Geirr's”) and ey (“island”).

tanche.etymology: From Old French tenche, from Late Latin tinca.

pitchi.etymology: From Old French pité, from Latin pietas, pietatem.

icône.etymology: From Latin īcon, from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn, “likeness, image, portrait”).

friser.etymology: From Old French friser, frizer (“to frizzle, crisp, curl, ruffle, braid, touch lightly, graze, scratch”), possibly from Frankish *fris (“curl”), from Proto-Germanic *frisaz (“frizzy, curly”).

secte.etymology: From Old French secte, from Late Latin secta (“a sect in philosophy or religion, a school, party, faction, class, gild, band, particularly a heretical doctrince or sect, etc.”), possibly from Latin sequor, sequī (“follow”).

pourpre.etymology: From Old French, from Latin purpura, from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra).

greffe.etymology: From Old French grefe, grafe, from Latin graphium.

glosses_en: Northern Ireland (a constituent country and province of the United Kingdom, situated in the northeastern part of the island of Ireland)

poulain.etymology: From Old French, from a Late Latin or Vulgar Latin pullamen, from Latin pullus (“animal young”).

ethnique.etymology: From Latin ethnicus (“pagan, heathen”), from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós, “of or for a nation, heathen”), from ἔθνος (éthnos, “a company", later "a people or nation, heathens”).

pédagogique.etymology: From Latin paedagogicus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγικός (paidagōgikós).

biau.etymology: From Old French biau, from Latin bellus.

cèdre.etymology: From Old French cedre, from Latin cedrus, from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros).

veir.etymology: From Old French vëoir, from Latin videō, vidēre, from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; see”).

glosses_en: Bermuda (an archipelago and overseas territory of the United Kingdom in the North Atlantic Ocean)

apostolique.etymology: From Latin apostolicus (“apostolic”), from Ancient Greek ἀποστολικός (apostolikós, “apostolic”).

allègre.etymology: From Old French halaigre, from Latin alacer (“lively; happy, joyful”).

glosses_en: To bring a wheelbarrow towards someone.

envieux.etymology: From Old French envious, envieus, from Latin invidiōsus.

hémorragie.etymology: From Latin haemorrhagia, from Ancient Greek αἱμορραγία (haimorrhagía, “a violent bleeding”), from αἱμορραγής (haimorrhagḗs, “bleeding violently”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + -ραγία (-ragía), from ῥηγνύναι (rhēgnúnai, “to break, burst”).

geai.etymology: From Old French jai (“jaybird, magpie”), from Late Latin gaius (“jaybird”).

cruche.etymology: From Old French cruche, from Frankish *krūkā.

glosses_en: Forming feminine nouns having the sense of ‘something contained by’ (the root word).

mulot.etymology: From Old French mul + -ot, from Old Dutch.

présider.etymology: From Old French presider, from Latin praesidēre (“to preside”), from pre- (“before”) + sedeō (“to sit”).

galactique.etymology: From Latin galacticus (“milky”), from Ancient Greek γαλακτικός (galaktikós).

ordonner.etymology: From Old French ordiner, borrowed from Latin ōrdinō, ōrdināre (“arrange, put in order; rule, govern; ordain, appoint to office”), from ōrdō (“methodical series, arrangement, or order; regular line, row, or series”) and influenced by donner.

heurter.etymology: From Old French hurter (“to ram into, strike, collide with”), from Frankish *hūrt (“a battering ram”), from Proto-Germanic *hrūtaną (“to fall, beat”), from Proto-Indo-European *krow- (“to fall, beat, break”).

pouls.etymology: From Old French, from Latin pulsus (“beat”), from pellō, pellere (“drive”).

goute.etymology: From Old French goute, gute, gote, from Latin gutta.

béni.etymology: From Old French beneïr, from Late Latin benedicō, benedīcere (“bless, praise”), from Latin benedicō, benedīcere (“speak well of someone, commend”).

glosses_en: a diminutive of the male given name Nic'lesse or Nicolas

milice.etymology: From Latin mīlitia (“military, military service”), from mīles (“soldier”).

assailli.etymology: From Old French assaillir, assalir, from Late Latin assalīre.

itou.etymology: Probably an alteration of Old French atout (“with”), influenced by itel (“such”).

sonder.etymology: From Old French sonder, from sonde (“sounding line”), from Old English [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *sundą (“a swim, body of water, sound”), from Proto-Indo-European *swem(bh)- (“to be unsteady, swim”).

grandement.etymology: Regularisation of Old French granment; by surface analysis, grand + -ment.

couchier.etymology: From Old French couchier, from Latin collocāre (“set in place”).

oïr.etymology: From Old French oir, from Latin audire (“to hear”).

rouai.etymology: From Old French roi, from Latin rēx, rēgem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs (“ruler, king”).

mesme.etymology: From Old French meïsme, mesme, from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, from Latin -met (intensifier) + ipse (“him/her/itself”) + -issimus (superlative ending).

bouter.etymology: From Old French bouter, of Germanic origin.

dreit.etymology: From Old French dreit, from Late Latin drictus, from Latin dīrēctus.

papillote.etymology: From Latin pāpiliō (compare French papillon, with the same meaning).

barbu.etymology: From Old French barbu, from Vulgar Latin *barbūtus (“bearded”). By surface analysis, barbe (“beard”) + -u. Compare French barbu.

glosses_en: a female given name from the Germanic languages

gardin.etymology: From Old Northern French gardin, Medieval Latin gardinus (“garden”) or oblique form of *gard, from Old Norse garðr (“yard, garden”), from Proto-Germanic *gardô, from *gardaz (“yard”). Compare French jardin, from Old French jardin.

soûl.etymology: From Latin satullus, diminutive of satur (“saturated”).

biauté.etymology: From Old French biauté, from Vulgar Latin *bellitātem.

marjolaine.etymology: From Old French majorane, from Medieval Latin maiorana.

mercie.etymology: From Old French merci (“mercy; clemency”), from Latin mercēs, mercēdem (“wages, fee, price”).

fieu.etymology: From Old French fil, itself from Latin filius.

moustrer.etymology: From Old French monstrer, moustrer, from Latin mōnstrō, mōnstrāre (“show”), from moneō, monēre (“warn, advise; remind”).

changier.etymology: From Old French changier. Cognate with Old French changer.

tolir.etymology: From Old French tolir, itself from Latin tollere.

graduel.etymology: From Medieval Latin graduālis, from Latin gradus (“step”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰradʰ-, *gʰredʰ- (“to walk, go”).

creire.etymology: From Old French creire, croire, from Latin crēdere (“to believe”).

apoplexie.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin apoplexia, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξία (apoplēxía).

orains.etymology: Inherited from Old French orainz, from Latin hora + antes.

bailli.etymology: From Old French baillier, from Latin bāiulāre (“to carry a burden”), from bāiulus (“one who bears burdens, porter, carrier”).

plenté.etymology: From Old French plenté, itself from Latin plenitas.

pèrdre.etymology: From Old French perdre, from Latin perdō, perdere.

weze.etymology: From Old French oisel, from Late Latin aucellus m (“little bird”), a diminutive ultimately based on Latin avis f (“bird”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis.

vanné.etymology: From Old French vanniel (compare French vanneau).

rituel.etymology: Borrowed from French rituel, from Latin rītuālis, from rītuum (“rite”) + -ālis.

acti.etymology: From Old French actif, from Latin āctīvus, from agō, agere (“do, act”).

peisson.etymology: From Old French poisson, itself from Latin piscis.

Jèrri.etymology: From Old Norse, compound of Geirs (“Geirr's”) and ey (“island”).

maîson.etymology: From Old French maisun, from Latin mansiō (“abode, home, dwelling”).

Dgèrnésy.etymology: Borrowed from Old Norse [Term?], a compound of Granis (“Grani's”) and ey (“island”).

tchaîse.etymology: From Old Northern French [Term?] (compare Old French chaiere), from Latin cathedra (“seat”), from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”).

lichon.etymology: From Old Northern French [Term?] (compare French leçon), from Latin lēctiō, lēctiōnem.

glosses_en: sedative (an agent or drug that sedates)
sédatif.etymology: Borrowed from French sédatif, from Medieval Latin sedātīvus.

glosses_en: to rub in soapy water, give a good scrub

Mêcrédi.etymology: From Old French mercredi, from Latin Mercuriī diēs, variant of diēs Mercuriī (“day of Mercury”).

liéthe.etymology: From Old French lire (compare French lire), from Latin legō, legere (“read, recite”).

glosses_en: of, from, or relating to Sark

ouvrer.etymology: From Old French ovrer (“to work”), from Late Latin operō, operāre, from the deponent Classical Latin verb operor, operārī (“work, labor”), from opus (“work, accomplishment”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep-os- (“work”), from the verbal root

Nouormand.etymology: From Old French normant, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą (“north”) and *mann- (“human being, man”).

glosses_en: France (a country located primarily in Western Europe)

housse.etymology: From Old French hous, hos, houlx (“holly”), from Frankish *hulis (“holly”).

samdi.etymology: Inherited from Old French samedi, from Vulgar Latin *sambatī diēs, from Latin Sabbatī diēs < diēs Sabbatī (“day of the Sabbath, Sabbath day”).

kien.etymology: From Old French kien, itself from Latin canis.

meis.etymology: From Old Northern French meis, from Latin mēnsis, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s.

veie.etymology: Inherited from Old French voie, from Latin via, from Proto-Italic *wiā, from Proto-Indo-European *weyh₁-.

viage.etymology: From Old French voiage, viage, veiage, from Latin viāticum, from via (“road”).

galetas.etymology: From Old French galatas (“housing in the upper part of a building”), from the tower of Galata, in Constantinople.

moûque.etymology: From an Old Northern French variant of Old French musche, mousche, from Latin musca.

freid.etymology: From Old French freid, from Latin frīgidus (through a contracted Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form fridus or frigdus, fricdus), from frīgeō, frīgēre (“be cold”).

venderdi.etymology: From Old French vendredi, from Latin Veneris diēs, variant of diēs Veneris.

baillier.etymology: From Old French baillier, from Latin bāiulāre (“to carry a burden”), from bāiulus (“one who bears burdens, porter, carrier”).

lyer.etymology: From Old French lire (compare French lire), from Latin legō, legere (“read, recite”).

manté.etymology: From Old Northern French [Term?] (compare French manteau), from Latin mantellum, diminutive of mantum, probably from Gaulish *mantos, *mantalos (“trodden road”), from Proto-Celtic *mantos, *mantlos, from Proto-Indo-European *menH- (“tread,

baté.etymology: From Old French batel, from Old English bāt, from Proto-Germanic *baitaz.

ieune.etymology: From Old French une, from Latin ūna, feminine of ūnus.

nièr.etymology: From Old French noir, neir, from Latin nigrum.

blianc.etymology: From Old French blanc, from Early Medieval Latin blancus, from Frankish *blank.

vêpre.etymology: From an Old Northern French variant of Old French vespe, guespe, wespe, from Latin vespa, possibly with Germanic influence. Compare French guêpe. Cf. also Norwegian veps, Danish hveps.

paîsson.etymology: From Old French poisson, peisson, from earlier peis, from Latin piscis, piscem, from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-.

ouaîsé.etymology: From Old French oisel, from Late Latin aucellus m (“little bird”), a diminutive ultimately based on Latin avis f (“bird”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis.

signeu.etymology: From Old French seignor, seignur, etc.

persoune.etymology: From Old French persone (compare French personne), from Latin persōna.

vassa.etymology: From Old French vassal, from Early Medieval Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from vassus (“servant”), from Gaulish uassos (“young man, squire”).

neir.etymology: From Old French neir, from Latin niger.

marchier.etymology: From Old French marchier, from Frankish *markōn.

fau.etymology: From Old French fau (“beech”), from Latin fagus.

rouage.etymology: From Old French roge, from Latin rubeus.

iun.etymology: From Old French uns, from Latin ūnus (“one”).

caeir.etymology: From Old French caeir, from older cadeir, from Vulgar Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre.

courtine.etymology: From Old French cortine, from Late Latin cōrtīna (“curtain”).

jugi.etymology: From Old French juger, from Latin iūdicō, iūdicāre (“pass judgement”).

capelain.etymology: From Old French capelain, from Late Latin cappellānus (“chaplain”), from cappella (“chapel”).

raisoun.etymology: From Old French raisun, itself from Latin ratio.

chent.etymology: From Old Northern French chent (Old French cent), from Latin centum, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.

Hippolyte.etymology: From Latin Hippolytus, from Ancient Greek Ἱππόλυτος (Hippólutos).

quate.etymology: From Old French quatre, from Latin quattuor, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres.

Rou.etymology: Also Rouf. From Old Norse Hrólfr.

capé.etymology: From Old Northern French capel, from Early Medieval Latin cappellus, diminutive from Late Latin cappa.

noueux.etymology: From Old French noous, from Latin nōdōsus.

vèr.etymology: From Old French verm (“worm”), from Latin vermis (“worm”).

burre.etymology: From Old French bure, from Latin būtȳrum, from Ancient Greek βούτῡρον (boútūron).

miton.etymology: From Old French miton, of Germanic origin.

drein.etymology: Old French drain, variant of derrain (“last”).

sacrément.etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin sacrāmentum (“sacrament”), from Latin sacrō (“to hallow, consecrate”), from sacer (“sacred, holy”).

molène.etymology: From Old French moleine, from Transalpine Gaulish melina (“yellow”).

Messie.etymology: From Latin Messias, from Ancient Greek Μεσσίας (Messías).

Sosthène.etymology: From Ancient Greek Σωσθένης (Sōsthénēs, “safe in strength”) the name of a Corinth Christian synagogue ruler, Σωσθένης.

Pentecôte.etymology: From Late Latin pentēcostē, from Ancient Greek πεντηκοστή (pentēkostḗ, “fiftieth (day)”).

gabé.etymology: From Middle French gabie (“foretop”), a borrowing from Old Occitan gabia (literally “cage, open framework, lantern of a bell tower”), from Latin cavea (“cage”), see also Italian gabbia (“hutch, cage”).

fach.etymology: From Old French fache, from Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“face, shape”).

vîn.etymology: From Old French vin, from Latin vīnum, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom.

glosses_en: a male given name, equivalent to French Mabille

faer.etymology: From Old French fer, from Latin ferrum.

vaie.etymology: From Old French vëoir, from Latin videō, vidēre, from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“to know; to see”).

pid.etymology: From Old French pié, from Latin pēs, pedis, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds.

fraid.etymology: From Old French freid, froit, from Latin frīgidus (“cold, cool, chilling”) (through a contracted Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form fridus or frigdus, fricdus), from frīgeō, frīgēre (“be cold”).

grev.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grava (attested in Medieval Latin; compare French grève), of pre-Latin origin.

crouaix.etymology: From Old French crois, from Latin crux, crucem, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”).

kérouaïe.etymology: From Old French crois, from Latin crux, crucem, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”).

mégabouochie.etymology: méga- + bouochie (“bite”), calque of English megabyte.

bouoche.etymology: From Old French boche, buche, from Latin bucca.

caûd.etymology: From Old Northern French caut, from Latin cal(i)dus.

gardîn.etymology: From Old Northern French gardin, diminutive (compare Vulgar Latin hortus gardinus) or oblique form of *gard, from Old Norse garðr (“yard, garden”), from Proto-Germanic *gardô, from *gardaz (“yard”). Compare French jardin, from Old French ja

bachîn.etymology: From Old French bachin, bacin, probably of Gaulish [Term?] origin.

faichon.etymology: From Old Northern French fechoun (compare Old French faceon, fazon, façon, whence the modern French word), from Latin factiō, factiōnem.

motchi.etymology: From Old French moquer, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mukkijaną, *mūhaną (“to low, bellow, shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *mūg-, *mūk- (“to low, mumble”).

dgide.etymology: From Old French guide, from Old Occitan guida, from guidar, from Frankish *witan (“to show the way”).

chaose.etymology: From Old French chose, from Latin causa.

aonclle.etymology: From Old French oncle, from Vulgar Latin *(av)unclus, from Latin avunculus.

acataïr.etymology: From Old Northern French acater, from Vulgar Latin *accaptāre (“accept, purchase”). Compare French acheter.

apportaïr.etymology: From Latin apportāre (“to bring, carry, conduct or convey to”), from ad + portō (“to carry, bear”).

arrêtaïr.etymology: From Old French arester (“to stay, stop”), from Vulgar Latin *arrestō, *arrestāre, from Latin ad- + restō, restāre (“to stop, remain behind, stay back”).

caontinuaïr.etymology: Borrowed from Latin continuāre (“to extend, prolong, continue”).

l'vaïr.etymology: From Old French lever, from Latin lēvō, levāre (“elevate”), from levis (“light, not heavy”).

r'paraïr.etymology: From Latin reparō, reparāre (“recover, retrieve; renew, restore, repair”).

trouvaïr.etymology: From Old French trover, truver, from Vulgar Latin *tropāre, from Latin tropus.

travaillier.etymology: From Old French travailler, from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“torment”), from Late Latin tripālium (“torture device”).

s'tcher.etymology: From Old French sechier, secher, from Latin siccō, siccāre, from siccus (“dry”).

méfiaïr.etymology: From mé- + Old French fier (“to trust”) (compare French méfier).

s'maïr.etymology: From Old French semer, from Latin sēminō, sēmināre.

copaïr.etymology: From Old French coper, colper, from cop, colp, from Late Latin colpus (“stroke”), from Latin colaphus.

coûtaïr.etymology: From Old French coster, from Latin constāre.

creitre.etymology: From Old French creistre, from Latin crēscō, crēscere (“increase, rise, grow, thrive; multiply, augment”).

decidaïr.etymology: From Latin dēcīdō, dēcīdere (“cut off, decide”), from dē (“down from”) + caedō (“cut”).

d'màndaïr.etymology: From Old French demander, from Latin demandō, demandāre.

d'meuraïr.etymology: From Latin dēmorō, dēmorārī (compare French demeurer).

dounnaïr.etymology: From Old French doner, from Latin dōnō, dōnāre (“give a present; bestow, grant”), from dōnum (“gift, present”).

éprouvaïr.etymology: From é- + Old French prover (“to prove”) (compare French éprouver).

frottaïr.etymology: Probably from Latin frictāre, frequentative of fricō through its past participle frictus (“rubbed”).

frumaïr.etymology: From Old French fermer, from Latin firmō, firmāre (“close”).

lavaïr.etymology: From Old French laver, from Latin lavō, lavāre.

màncher.etymology: From Latin mancus (“maimed, powerless”) (compare French manquer).

muchier.etymology: From Old French muchier, mucier, mucer (“to skulk, hide, conceal”), from Frankish *mukkjan (“to hide, conceal oneself”), from Proto-Germanic *mukjaną, *mūkōną (“to hide, ambush”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mūg-, *(s)mewgʰ- (“swindler, th

oïmaïr.etymology: From the conjugated forms of Old French amer, aimer, from Latin amō, amāre (“love”).

ouir.etymology: From Old French oïr, from Latin audīre (“to hear, listen”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew-is-d-, from the root *h₂ew- (“to see, perceive”).

pâssaïr.etymology: From Old French passer, from Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step, pace”, noun).

pensaïr.etymology: From Old French penser, from Latin pēnsāre (“ponder, consider”).

portaïr.etymology: From Old French porter, from Latin portō, portāre.

pouôinturaïr.etymology: pouôinture (“paint, paintwork”) + -aïr (compare French peinturer, from peinture (“painting”))

ramassaïr.etymology: From re- + Old French amasser (“to amass; to gather up”).

maette.etymology: From Old French metre, from Latin mittō, mittere.

llierre.etymology: From Old French lire (compare French lire), from Latin legō, legere (“read, recite”).

Latîn.etymology: From Latin latīnus, from Latium (“the region around Rome”).

ch'fa.etymology: From Old French cheval, from Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), of disputed origin (compare Gaulish caballos (“horse”), Ancient Greek καβάλλης (kabállēs, “nag”)).

qùeva.etymology: From Old Northern French [Term?] (compare Old French cheval), from Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), of disputed origin (compare Gaulish caballos (“horse”), Ancient Greek καβάλλης (kabállēs, “nag”)).

fuule.etymology: From Old French fueille, from Late Latin folia, originally the plural of Latin folium.

fieille.etymology: From Old French fueille, from Late Latin folia, originally the plural of Latin folium.

leunmiéthe.etymology: From Medieval Latin lūmināria, neuter plural of lūmināre (“star”), ultimately from Classical Latin lūmen (“light”).

cŷngne.etymology: From Latin cygnus (“swan”); compare French cygne.

châté.etymology: From Old French chastel, from Latin castellum.

normaund.etymology: From Old French normant, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą (“north”) and *mann- (“human being, man”).

bliu.etymology: From Old French blöe, bleve, blef (“blue”), of Germanic origins.

vaert.etymology: From Old French vert, from Vulgar Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis. Cf. French vert, Italian verde and Spanish verde.

aîdgu.etymology: From Old French agu, from Latin acūtus (“sharp”).

aîsi.etymology: From Old French aisié (“eased, at ease, at leisure”), past participle of aisier (“to put at ease”), from aise (“empty space, elbow room, opportunity”), of uncertain origin.

apèrt.etymology: From Latin apertus (“having been opened; having been uncovered; frank, clear, manifest”), past participle of aperiō, aperīre (“open; uncover”).

avanchi.etymology: From Old French avanchir, from Late Latin ab ante, from Latin ab + ante (“before”).

aveugl'ye.etymology: From Old French avogle, from Late Latin ab oculis (“without eyes”).

bénîn.etymology: From Latin benignus (“kind, good”), from bonus (“good”) + genus (“origin, kind”).

bouôn.etymology: From Old French bon, from Latin bonus.

cèrtain.etymology: From Old French certain, from Vulgar Latin unattested form *certānus, extended form of Latin certus (“fixed, resolved, certain”).

cliai.etymology: From Old French cler, from Latin clārus.

compliet.etymology: From Old French complet, borrowed from Latin complētus.

continnuel.etymology: From Old French continuel, from Latin continuus (“continuous”).

crînminnel.etymology: From Old French criminal, from Late Latin crīminālis, from Latin crīmen (“crime”).

leçaon.etymology: Borrowed from French leçon, from Latin lēctiō, lēctiōnem.

maisaon.etymology: From Old French maisun, from Latin mansiō (“abode, home, dwelling”).

païssaon.etymology: From Old French poisson, peisson, from earlier peis, from Latin piscis, piscem, from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-.

tchuthieux.etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin cūriōsus (“careful, attentive, inquisitive”).

flleur.etymology: From Old French flor, flur, from Latin flōs, flōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“flower, blossom”).

faumme.etymology: From Old French fame, feme, fenme, femme, from Latin fēmina, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-eh₂ (“who sucks”), derivation of the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, suckle”).

f'nête.etymology: From Old French fenestre, from Latin fenestra.

naissànse.etymology: From Latin nāscentia, from nāscēns (“being born”), present active participle of nāscor (“to be born”).

haeure.etymology: From Old French ore, eure, from Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “time, season, year”).

bouais.etymology: Inherited from Old French bois, from Early Medieval Latin boscus (“grove”), borrowed from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz.

chendre.etymology: From an Old Northern French variant of Old French cendre (compare French cendre), from Latin cinis, cinerem, from Proto-Indo-European *ken- (“dust, ashes”).

chucre.etymology: From Old French çucre; see there for more.

charitaïe.etymology: From Old French charité, from Latin cāritās.

ch'min.etymology: From Old French chemin, from Vulgar Latin cammīnus (“way”), from Gaulish [Term?].

caoud.etymology: From Old Northern French caut, from Latin cal(i)dus.

choïne.etymology: From Old French chaeine, from Latin catēna, from Proto-Indo-European *kat- (“to link or weave together; chain, net”).

cliochi.etymology: Compare French clocher. Related to clioche (“bell”).

sablion.etymology: From Old French sablon, sablun, from Late Latin sablō, sablōnem, from Latin sabulō, sabulōnem (“coarse sand, gravel”).

crôteux.etymology: crôte (“crust”) + -eux; cf. also Latin crustosus and compare French croûteux.

difféthent.etymology: From Latin differēns, present active participle of differō, differre (“differ, be different”).

mârri.etymology: From Old French mari (“grieved, sad”), past participle of marir (“to get angry, become distressed”), from Frankish *marrijan, from Proto-Germanic *marzijaną (“to neglect, ignore, hinder, disturb, impede”), from Proto-Indo-European *mers- (“

ouvaert.etymology: From Old French overt, from Latin apertus, probably through a Vulgar Latin root *opertus.

cârré.etymology: From Latin quadrātus, perfect passive participle of quadrō, quadrāre (“make square”).

haout.etymology: From Old French hault, haut, halt (“high, tall, elevated”), a conflation of Frankish *hauh, *hōh (“high, tall, elevated”) and Latin altus (“high, raised, profound”).

êcliaithi.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *exclāriāre, from Latin exclārō, from ex- + clārō.

êlectrique.etymology: From Latin ēlectricus, from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron).

r'ligieux.etymology: From Old French religieus, from Latin religiōsus, from religiō. Cognate to French religieux.

r'pugnant.etymology: From Old French repugnant, borrowed from Latin repugnāns, present participle of repugnō, repugnāre (“oppose, fight against”).

êtèrnel.etymology: From Late Latin aeternālis (“everlasting, eternal”), from Latin aeternus (“eternal”).

êtrait.etymology: From Old Northern French estreit, (compare Old French estroit), from Latin strictus (“tightened, compressed, having been tightened”), perfect passive participle of stringō, stringere (“tighten, compress”), from Proto-Indo-European *streyg-.

rotchet.etymology: From Old Northern French rocquier (compare Old French rochier, modern French rocher).

chànge.etymology: From Old French change, from Gaulish cambion, *kambyom (“change”), from Proto-Celtic *kambos (“twisted, crooked”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱambos, *(s)kambos (“crooked”).

couraonne.etymology: From Old French corone, from Latin corōna, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē, “garland, wreath”).

faeu.etymology: From Old French feu, fou, from Latin focus (“hearth”).

fanmeux.etymology: From Old French fameus, from Latin fāmōsus, from fāma (“fame, reputation”).

futhieux.etymology: From Old French furieus, borrowed from Latin furiōsus (“full of madness or rage, furious, raging”).

ombreux.etymology: From Old French, from Latin umbrōsus. Equivalent to ombre (“shadow”) + -eux.

ordgilleux.etymology: From Old French orgoillus (“proud”), equivalent to ordgi (“pride”) + -eux (compare French orgueilleux).

génétheux.etymology: From Old French, from Latin generōsus.

grâcieux.etymology: From Old French gracieus, borrowed from Latin grātiōsus.

hèrbeux.etymology: From Latin herbōsus (compare hèrbe, French herbeux).

nèrveux.etymology: From Old French nerveus, from Latin nervōsus.

séthieux.etymology: From Old French serieux, from Medieval Latin sēriōsus, from Classical Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”).

trompeux.etymology: Related to French tromper (“to deceive”) ( + -eux), from a Germanic source.

prospéthe.etymology: From Old French, ultimately from Latin prosperus.

tchiède.etymology: From Old French tiede (compare French tiède), from Latin tepidus.

nécessaithe.etymology: From Old French necessaire, from Latin necessārius (“unavoidable, inevitable, indispensable, requisite”).

întînme.etymology: From Latin intimus (“inmost; profound; most or very secret or intimate”).

înmense.etymology: From Latin immēnsus, from in- (“without”) + mēnsūra (“measure, measuring”).

raichinne.etymology: From Old French, from Late Latin rādīcīna (“root”), from Latin rādīx, rādīcis (“root”), from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds.

innouothant.etymology: From Latin īgnōrāns (“unknowing, being ignorant of; ignoring, unheeding”), present active participle of īgnōrō (“to do not know; to be unacquainted with; to be ignorant of; to ignore”).

înstruithe.etymology: From Old French (compare French instruire), from Latin īnstruō, īnstruere.

êcole.etymology: From Old French escole, from Vulgar Latin *iscola, from Classical Latin schola.

taompette.etymology: From Old French tempeste, from Latin tempesta.

entchi.etymology: From Old French entier, from Latin integer, integrum.

êga.etymology: From Old French igal, remade from the popular inherited forms uel, evel, oel, ivel, based on their original etymology, Latin aequālis.

divèrs.etymology: From Latin dīversus (“opposite; separate, apart; diverse, different; hostile”).

êcars.etymology: From Old Northern French scars, escars, from Late Latin *scarsus, probably originally a participle form of *excarpō (“to take out”), from Latin ex- + carpō.

fanmilyi.etymology: From Latin familiāris (“familiar, intimate, friendly”), from familia (“household”).

janne.etymology: Inherited from Old French jane, jenne, juene, from Vulgar Latin *iŏvenem, from Latin iuvenem.

lîlas.etymology: Borrowed from French lilas, formerly lilac, from Arabic لِيلَك (līlak), from Persian نیلک (nilak), from نیل (nil, “dark blue”), ultimately from Sanskrit नीला (nīlā, “dark blue”).

partitchulyi.etymology: From Old French particulier, from Late Latin particulāris (“particular; partial”), from Latin particula (“small part, particle”), a diminutive of pars (“piece”).

mangnifique.etymology: From Old French magnifique, from Latin magnificus.

mucre.etymology: Borrowed from Old Norse mygla (“to grow musty”) or more probably Old Norse mykr (“dung”).

publyi.etymology: From Latin pūblicus (“pertaining to the people”).

preunmyi.etymology: From Old French premier, from Latin prīmārius.

rédgulyi.etymology: From Latin rēgulāris (“continuing rules for guidance”), from rēgula (“rule”).

rouoya.etymology: From Old French roial, from Latin rēgālis, from rēx (“king”).

êpais.etymology: From Old French espés, from Latin spissus (“thick, close, compact, dense, crowded”).

sîndgulyi.etymology: From Old French singuler, from Latin singulāris, from singulus (“single”).

sétchulyi.etymology: From Latin saeculāris (“worldly, temporal, profane”), from saeculum (“worldliness”).

pouôrre.etymology: From Old French povre, from Latin pauper, pauperem.

fèrme.etymology: From Old French ferm, ferme (“solid”), from Latin firmus (“solid, secure”).

înc'mode.etymology: From Latin incommodus, from in- + commodus (“convenient”).

habil'ye.etymology: From Old French habile, from Latin habilis (“suitable; apt”), from habeō (“to handle”).

seux.etymology: Old French seur, whence French sûr.

meux.etymology: From Old French meur (compare French mûr), from Latin mātūrus (“mature; ripe”).

aut'.etymology: From Old French altre, autre, from Latin alter, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élteros (“the other of two”).

îndividuel.etymology: From Medieval Latin indīviduālis, from Latin indīviduum (“an indivisible thing”), neuter of indīviduus (“indivisible, undivided”), from in + dīviduus (“divisible”), from dīvidō (“to divide”).

miyeu.etymology: From Old French mielz, mialz, miels, from Latin melius. Cf. French mieux.

étaï.etymology: From Old French esté, from Latin aestās, aestātem.

r'pas.etymology: From Old French repast, from the verb repaistre (“to eat”).

qualitaï.etymology: From Old French qualité, from Latin quālitas, quālitātem.

saembole.etymology: From Latin symbolus, symbolum, from Ancient Greek σύμβολον (súmbolon).

finnal.etymology: From Old French final, from Latin fīnālis, from fīnis (“end, limit”).

frîngant.etymology: From an Old French present participle of the verb fringuer (“to jump, leap; to frolic, gambol, caper; to caress a woman; to rinse”).

împâtient.etymology: From Latin impatiēns, from im- + patiēns (“patient”).

leuné.etymology: Related to leune (“moon”); compare French luné, from lune (“moon”).

mouoilli.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *molliāre (“to soften by soaking”), from Latin mollia, a substantive form of the adjective mollis (“soft”).

ouvèrt.etymology: From Old French overt, from Latin apertus, probably through a Vulgar Latin root *opertus.

pâcient.etymology: From Old French pacient, borrowed from Latin patiēns, patientis.

pliaîsant.etymology: From Old French plaisant, present participle of plaire (“to please”).

pliat.etymology: From Old French, from Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat”).

préchain.etymology: From Old French prochain, from proche, from Latin proximus.

prêssi.etymology: From Latin pressō (“to press, squeeze”), frequentative of premō (“to press; to pursue”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to hit”).

r'calcitrant.etymology: From Latin recalcitrāns, recalcitrantis, present participle of recalcitrō, recalcitrāre (“be disobedient”).

s'gret.etymology: From Old French secret, from Latin sēcrētus.

tchuit.etymology: From an Old Northern French variant of Old French cuit, from Latin coctus.

teurt.etymology: From Old French, from Latin tortus.

étourné.etymology: From Old French esturnel, from Late Latin sturnellus, from Latin sturnus, from Proto-Indo-European *storo (“starling”).

graïve.etymology: Uncertain. Possibly from the feminine form of Old French grieu, griu, from Latin graecus (“Greek”), the thrush being a migratory bird that had hivernated in Greece.

maoue.etymology: From Old French mave (“mew”), from Old English mǣw (“mew, seagull”), from Proto-Germanic *maihwaz, *maiwaz (“seagull”).

nouaix.etymology: From Old French nois, from Latin nux, nucem.

pllie.etymology: From Old French pluie, from Vulgar Latin *ploia < *plovia, from Classical Latin pluvia.

saisaon.etymology: From Old French seson, seison (“time of sowing, seeding”), from Latin satiōnem, accusative of satiō (“act of sowing, planting”) from satum, past participle of serō (“to sow, plant”) from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“to sow, plant”).

bliond.etymology: From Old French blond, blont, from Frankish *blund (“a mixed color between golden and light-brown”).

boête.etymology: From Late Latin buxida, late form of Latin pyxis, pyxidem, from Ancient Greek πυξίς (puxís, “box”).

dgiâbl'ye.etymology: From Old French diable, deable, a semi-learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin or Late Latin diabolus, from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).

valentîn.etymology: From la Saint Valentîn (“St. Valentine's Day”).

rocque.etymology: From Old Northern French roque, from Early Medieval Latin rocca (767), of uncertain origin. Compare French roche from Old French roche. Compare also English rock.

traithe.etymology: From Old French treire, traire, from Vulgar Latin *tragere, from Latin trahō, trahere (“pull”, verb).

guénipe.etymology: From Old Norse kvinna (“woman”) (compare French guenipe).

riviéthe.etymology: From Old French riviere, from Early Medieval Latin rīpāria.

g'linne.etymology: From Old French geline, from Vulgar Latin *galina, from Latin gallīna (“hen”), from gallus (“rooster”).

poulette.etymology: From Old French, equivalent to poule (“hen”) + -ette (diminutive suffix).

pâlle.etymology: From Old French paille, from Latin palea.

païle.etymology: From Old French paille, from Latin palea.

boutelle.etymology: From Old French boteille, from Late Latin butticula.

clios.etymology: From Old French clos (“enclosed outdoor area; field, paddock”), from Latin clausus.

vèrre.etymology: From Old French voirre, from Latin vitrum.

m'lon.etymology: From Old French melon, from Late Latin melonem, from Latin melopeponem (“type of pumpkin”), from Ancient Greek μηλοπέπων (mēlopépōn), from μῆλον (mêlon, “apple”) + πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”).

couôtuthe.etymology: From Vulgar Latin consutura, ultimately from Latin cōnsuō (“to sew, stitch, join”) (compare couôtre (“to sew”)).

courtil.etymology: From Old French cortil, itself from Medieval Latin curtilis.

denchive.etymology: From Old French [Term?], from Latin gingīva, altered under influence from dent (“tooth”).

hitre.etymology: From Old French oistre, uistre, from Latin ostrea, from Ancient Greek ὄστρεον (óstreon).

f'nêtre.etymology: From Old French fenestre, from Latin fenestra.

rueûque.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin rusca (“bark”), from Gaulish rusca, from Proto-Celtic *rūskos (“bark”).

tâsse.etymology: From Old French tasse, from Arabic طَاس (ṭās) (a shortening of طَسْت (ṭast)), from Middle Persian tšt' (tašt).

frouque.etymology: From Old Northern French forque (compare Old French forche), from Latin furca (“pitchfork, forked stake”, also “gallows, beam, stake, support post, yoke”), of uncertain origin.

ich'in.etymology: From Northern Old French chi (“here”), from Late Latin ecce hīc, with /i-/ added by analogy with Old French iluec (“there, in that place”), from Latin illoc.

étout.etymology: Probably an alteration of Old French atout (“with”), influenced by itel (“such”).

vèrgue.etymology: From Latin virga (“shoot, rod stick”) (compare Middle French verge (“rod or wand of office”)), of unknown origin.
